one_pager.big_idea: Our brains take shortcuts that can fool us, so scientists measure, compare groups and try to prove their own ideas wrong.
goals: I can show with measurements that my perception can be wrong, and explain why scientists measure instead of trusting their eyes.
I can explain anchoring and confirmation bias using evidence from today's class tests.

flow.what: Anchoring slips handed out from the pre-shuffled pile as students arrive (Versions 1 and 2 alternate): 'Answer alone, in silence, then fold it.' Slips go into the group envelopes. Then the retrieval question: 'Hot water freezes faster than cold water': claim type and the three verdicts. Slides 1 to 2.

Muller-Lyer lines: vote A longer, B longer or the same; do not reveal and do not measure yet. Students write their prediction on the worksheet. The teacher quietly sorts the slips into Version 1 and Version 2 piles using the code in the corner. Slide 3.

Perception versus measurement; what bias means (a pull in one direction, three brain traps: eyes, numbers, looking only for 'yes'); how to measure to the nearest millimetre: start at 0, eyes directly above the mark. Do not mention anchoring yet. Slides 4 to 6.

Illusion sheets given out. Pairs predict, then measure the illusions and complete Core ('Measure, don't look!'). Two quick-finishing Recorders get the two piles of slips, the tally sheet and a calculator and work out the class means. Slide 7. If short: cut bonus illusion C (Lines E and F); teacher computes the means.

2-4-6 game from the script: groups test three numbers each round and record on the group card; the teacher answers only 'Yes' or 'No' and writes every test on the board in YES and NO columns; reveal the rule (any three numbers in increasing order) and name confirmation bias. Slides 8 to 9. If short: 3 rounds instead of 5.

Reveal the anchoring trick and the two class means; compare with the true length (about 6,300 km). 'How do scientists protect themselves from bias?': pair talk in any language, share with a frame; Stretch or Challenge if time; exit ticket and logbook line. Slides 10 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Pairs predict, then measure three optical illusions with a 30 cm ruler to the nearest mm (A and B 80 mm, C and D 20 mm, E and F 60 mm). Groups then play the 2-4-6 game, testing sets of three numbers to find a secret rule. A hidden two-version Do Now slip gives class data on anchoring.
one_pager.assessment: Exit ticket (strip at the foot of the worksheet): can the student name a bias and a protection against it, and choose the test that best checks 'add 2' (b: 1, 2, 3)? Logbook line under 'What I found': 'My brain was fooled when ___.' The bias reflection in the My thinking box is the series output for this week.
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'My eyes said ___, but the ruler showed ___.' 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'This could also be explained by ___.' Chinese talk is welcome in pair talk and in the 2-4-6 group discussions; tests are called out in English numbers; the My thinking box may be in any language. Traps: 'bias' is often heard as 'unfair person', but here it is any pull in one direction, including in data; the key word table gives two Chinese terms for bias, one for results and one for people; 'estimate' is not a wild guess.
watch_out: Do not mention anchoring or the two versions before the Think phase, or the test is spoiled; say only 'Answer alone, in silence, then fold it.'
Print the illusion sheets at 100% and check A and B measure 80 mm; if the printer has scaled them, the answer key values change.

Many students learn the Yangtze's length (about 6,300 km) in geography: if the two means are close, treat it as a result, not a failure, or use the sample data in the answer key if class data is unusable.
Misconceptions: 'Clever people are not fooled'; 'If many tests say yes, the idea is proven'; 'A ruler gives an exact answer' (measuring is only good to about 1 mm).
In the 2-4-6 game do not reveal the rule or comment on the nearly empty NO column until the end; to a wrong rule say only 'That is not my rule. Keep testing.'
